📌 Address Poisoning: Why Your Transaction History Can Lie

Main Points
⏺ Scammers plant look-alike addresses in your wallet history
⏺ One careless copy-paste sends your funds to them
⏺ This post explains how the trick works and how to avoid it



1️⃣ Core Idea — Attackers create an address that starts and ends with the same characters as one you use, then send you a tiny or zero-value transfer from it so it shows up in your history.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Most people check only the first and last few characters, and many wallets shorten addresses on screen. Copying "the last address I used" from history is a habit scammers count on.
3️⃣ Example — You regularly send USDT to your exchange. A dust transfer arrives from an address that looks the same at a glance; next time you copy from history and pick the fake one.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Stablecoin transfers, wallets that display shortened addresses, and any payment you copy from recent activity instead of a saved contact.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Never copy addresses from your transaction history. Use a saved address book, check the full address, and send a small test transfer before a large one.
Final Thoughts

Address poisoning doesn't hack your wallet — it hacks your attention. A few extra seconds of checking is the whole defense.

The Tip Behind Netanyahu’s Stolen-Election Warning

On Election Day, Benjamin Netanyahu pointed to the arrests of three Ra’am activists and warned voters, “They are trying to steal the elections from us.” He did not mention that his own chief of staff and a former aide had helped set the arrests in motion, The New York Times reports.

Police said they suspected a plot to bribe voters and had seized envelopes of cash. Ra’am denied the allegation. Police later acknowledged in court that they had searched at least two homes without warrants. All three men were released without charge.

The judge who ordered one activist’s release noted that the file showed him campaigning for Ra’am and taking part in meetings with candidates. “But that’s not a crime,” the judge added.

Netanyahu’s office initially denied reports that police acted on a tip from chief of staff Ido Norden. After a Channel 12 investigation, the office acknowledged that Norden had passed along information and said he had acted “like any other citizen.”

A lawyer for former Netanyahu aide Daniel Greenberg confirmed his client was the source of the tip and denied that he had tried to improperly influence the vote. The attorney general and state prosecutor are looking into the matter.

Arab-led parties won a record 19 of the Knesset’s 120 seats. Election officials say there is no proof of widespread fraud that could have affected the result.

Whether anyone improperly influenced the police is still an open question. What is already on the record is how the arrests were used. Netanyahu’s chief of staff passed the tip to police, and Netanyahu presented the arrests as evidence that others were trying to steal the vote.

📣 MEXC shuts down Visa-linked crypto card less than three months after launch 

🌐 Cryptocurrency exchange MEXC has announced that it will discontinue its Global Card payment services on Nov. 18 at 15:30 UTC, less than two weeks after U.S. authorities issued an order restricting its access to the American financial system. The exchange did not identify the issuing partner or specify whether its decision was directly related to the recent enforcement action by the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

📊 During the maintenance period, customers could transfer their remaining card balances to their exchange accounts, while transactions initiated before the suspension remained subject to normal settlement procedures. MEXC had initially described the interruption as temporary but has now confirmed that the service will not resume as scheduled.

🔗 Cardholders could receive cashback ranging from 4% to 10%, with monthly rewards capped at up to 800 USDT depending on their eligibility. Applications were already unavailable to U.S. residents under the exchange’s regional restrictions. Customers using the card for recurring payments have been advised to cancel their subscriptions or register alternative payment methods to avoid interruptions once the card becomes inactive.

In a study of 29 experienced Vipassana meditators, deeper meditation made brain responses to ordinary sounds more consistent and easier for machine-learning tools to distinguish from background activity.

Harvard researcher Timothy Lomas proposes that reduced neural noise might allow faint signals into awareness, potentially explaining reports of extrasensory perception. The idea remains speculative: the Oxford-led study tested only sound processing, and both papers are non-peer-reviewed preprints. Neuroscientist David Vago cautions that anecdotes alone cannot establish scientific consensus.

[Nath, M., Reggente, N., Bailey, N., Kringelbach, M., & Laukkonen, R. (2026). Meditation Depth Enhances the Functional Signal-to-Noise Ratio of the Brain [Preprint]. bioRxiv. DOI: 10.64898/2026.06.30.735351]
